name: epics-base
desc: Experimental Physics and Industrial Control System
why: Industrial control system toolkit for physics labs; the real-time device protocol is a fascinating door, but it is heavy and needs hardware to shine.

brief.what_it_is: EPICS (Experimental Physics and Industrial Control System) is a set of software tools and applications for building distributed control systems to operate devices such as particle accelerators, large experiments and major telescopes. The README describes EPICS Base as the central core of that control system toolkit. Built from source, it provides a soft IOC (Input/Output Controller) that runs a Channel Access server, and the records it serves are listed from an interactive epics> prompt. The homepage's own description says such systems can span tens or hundreds of networked computers, controlled from a central room or remotely.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames EPICS as software infrastructure so that large, distributed control systems can be built without starting from scratch, since such systems typically involve many networked computers that must communicate and provide feedback. The homepage also says EPICS 7 expands it beyond the process control layer, adding a structured data system and an efficient data transfer protocol (pvAccess) for applications that need higher abstraction.
brief.how_it_works: Per the README, you download a release from the Downloads page, unpack it, and run make to build. After building, an example soft IOC is started with a single command that serves Channel Access, and its records can be listed by typing dbl at the epics> prompt. The homepage adds that EPICS 7's pvAccess protocol carries the newer structured data. The README does not explain the record or database model in detail.

commands_seen.context: Run inside the unpacked release folder to build EPICS Base after downloading a release.
Starts the example soft IOC after building; the README says it runs a Channel Access server. The -x first argument sets the prefix for the records.
Typed at the epics> prompt of the running softIoc; lists the records it provides (the README example shows first:BaseVersion and first:exit).

brief.install_notes: Install is from source: download a release from the epics-controls.org Downloads page, unpack, and run make. The README points to the documentation's Installation page for system-specific instructions, which I did not fetch. The Homebrew formula's caveats (from the package metadata, not the README) say that to use EPICS in a shell you must set EPICS_BASE to $HOMEBREW_PREFIX/opt/epics-base/libexec and EPICS_HOST_ARCH from the output of the EpicsHostArch.pl script. The formula installs client and server executables including caget, caput, camonitor, pvget, pvput, pvmonitor, softioc and softiocpva. No hardware, account, or runtime requirements appeared in the README.
brief.standout: A control-system toolkit that runs as a software IOC on an ordinary machine, so the basic Channel Access server can be tried without any hardware. Its open license and long use at scientific facilities give it an unusual pedigree for open-source software.
brief.status: Maintained, based on the homepage: it lists news items dated 2026 and upcoming events (a Developers Meeting and Codeathon in October 2026, a Collaboration Meeting in November 2026, and a Summer School in August 2026). The README has no release date or last-commit date that I could see, so this is an inference, not a verified commit date.
brief.caveats: The README gives no platform list beyond the build steps; the Homebrew caveat implies a Unix-style shell setup. Licensing is described two ways: the homepage says EPICS Open License, while the README points to a Software License Agreement in a LICENSE file, which I did not open. The README's example depends on building from source, and the tools are aimed at large distributed systems, so a small test is possible but the full feature set is heavy. The homepage was a general marketing site rather than a technical page, so detail came mostly from the README. Quick-start commands were taken from the README only.

entry.title: EPICS Base
entry.tldr: The control-system toolkit behind particle accelerators and telescopes, which runs as a soft IOC on your laptop so you can poke at it with no hardware.
entry.deeper_look:
EPICS (Experimental Physics and Industrial Control System) is a set of software tools for building distributed control systems that operate devices such as particle accelerators, large experiments and major telescopes. EPICS Base is the core of that toolkit. The homepage describes systems that can span tens or hundreds of networked computers, run from a central room or remotely.

The central piece is the IOC, the Input/Output Controller. An IOC serves named records over a network protocol called Channel Access, and clients read, write or subscribe to those names. The Homebrew formula installs both sides: server programs like `softioc`, and client tools like `caget`, `caput` and `camonitor`. A soft IOC is the same server running on an ordinary computer with no instruments attached, which makes it a way to see the model without a lab.

It exists so that labs do not have to build control infrastructure from scratch. Many networked computers need to communicate and give feedback, and EPICS supplies that layer. EPICS 7 adds a structured data system and a newer protocol, pvAccess, served by the `pv*` tools (`pvget`, `pvput`, `pvmonitor`, `pvlist`). The homepage says it enables applications that need higher abstraction.

The door here is the idea of a control system as named values on a network, with every device, sensor and setpoint addressable the same way. The README does not explain the record and database model in detail, so expect to lean on the documentation after the first example.
entry.install:
brew install epics-base
# Add to your shell configuration:
export EPICS_BASE=$HOMEBREW_PREFIX/opt/epics-base/libexec
export EPICS_HOST_ARCH=$($HOMEBREW_PREFIX/opt/epics-base/bin/EpicsHostArch.pl)

try_this.what_happens: Shows the options of the soft IOC server, which serves records over Channel Access without any hardware.
Shows how to read the value of a named record from a running IOC.
Shows the pvAccess client, the EPICS 7 counterpart for fetching structured data.

entry.whats_unique: It is control-system software with a long record at scientific facilities, and it runs as a software IOC on an ordinary machine. You can try the server side without a lab.
entry.caveats: The tools are aimed at large distributed systems, so a small test works but the full feature set is heavy, and the README's own example builds from source rather than via Homebrew.
